language.note: Emirati Arabic, or Al Ramsa, belongs to the Gulf Arabic group; Modern Standard Arabic is used in school and official documents.

culture_note: The majlis, a sitting room and family gathering place, has been listed by UNESCO as intangible cultural heritage since 2015. Arabic coffee is served with dates, and pouring for the guest first is a mark of honour.
people_note: Receive and give things with the right hand. Shoes are removed before entering a home or a majlis. Guests greet the eldest person first. With the opposite gender, wait for the woman to offer her hand first.

story.text: When a guest steps into the majlis, the cushion-lined sitting room, the host in the United Arab Emirates serves Arabic coffee. It is poured from a dallah, a long-necked brass pot, into a small handleless cup called a finjan. Dates are set beside it to offset the bitterness. The cup is filled only halfway, and the guest receives it with the right hand, then returns it the same way; declining a refill is done with a slight hand gesture. Everyday speech here is Emirati Arabic, which its speakers call Al Ramsa and which belongs to the Gulf Arabic group. In school and official documents, Modern Standard Arabic is used. The sound q, pronounced q in Standard Arabic, becomes g in this dialect, so qahwa is heard as gahwa. The majlis itself, a sitting room and family gathering place, has been listed by UNESCO as intangible cultural heritage since 2015.

language.note: Kuwaiti Arabic belongs to the Gulf group; its vocabulary absorbed Persian, Turkish, English, and Hindi words through the country's maritime and trading history.

culture_note: The diwaniya, a separate front sitting room, is where men gather to discuss family and neighbourhood matters. Hosting guests is seen as an honour, so coffee and dates are served before long conversation.
people_note: Begin with the eldest when greeting. Use the right hand to eat and to give. Accepting the coffee served honours the host. Relaxed talk and shared stories are common in social life.

story.text: In Kuwait, male guests are often received in the diwaniya, a separate front room set aside for gatherings. Arabic coffee is poured from a pot and served with dates; the guest accepts the small cup with the right hand. Everyday speech is Kuwaiti Arabic, part of the Gulf Arabic group. The old port city of Kuwait was a trading crossroads, so its dialect absorbed many words from Persian, Turkish, English, and Hindi. Its distinctive sounds are easy to hear: q becomes g and k becomes ch, including in qahwa, heard as gahwa. Kuwait's soap-opera industry made this accent familiar as far away as Tunisia and Jordan. Society is diglossic: Modern Standard Arabic serves school and administration, while Kuwaiti Arabic is used at home and is seen as a marker of identity.

language.note: Lebanese Arabic belongs to the Levantine Arabic group; French loanwords are common because of history and education.

culture_note: Hosting is seen as an honour, so dinner invitations often come early in a friendship. Lateness is tolerated: about twenty minutes is still considered normal, and guests usually bring sweets.
people_note: Greet the household in order of age, starting with the eldest. Accept offered tea or coffee as a sign of respect. Avoid crossing your legs so your foot points at someone.

story.text: In Beirut, guests arriving at a home usually greet the household in order of age, starting with the oldest. The host serves Levantine coffee, finely ground and scented with cardamom, brewed in a long-handled pot called a rakwa. In rural areas and Bedouin camps, a larger long-spouted pot known as a bakraj is used. Before modern cafes spread, Arab coffeehouses served as places of discussion; some called them schools of the wise. The official language is Modern Standard Arabic, but daily talk uses Lebanese Arabic, part of the Levantine group, often mixed with French words. Speakers therefore switch easily between two registers. Guest etiquette expects visitors to taste every dish served as a sign of respect. Refusing an offer of coffee or tea can seem to slight the host's honour, so accepting is considered more polite.

culture_note: The khanjar, a curved dagger, is worn by Omani men at weddings and national occasions; its craft and customs were inscribed by UNESCO in 2022. Omani coffee is scented with cardamom and served with dates or halwa.
people_note: Receive and give with the right hand. Guests greet the eldest person first. At a gathering, the food served should be tasted. Honorific titles for elders are common as a mark of good manners.

story.text: In Muscat, a host welcomes guests with Omani coffee served alongside dates or halwa, a chewy sweet. The coffee is poured from a dallah, a long-spouted pot, into small cups; guests receive and return the cup with the right hand. Omani men wear the khanjar, a curved dagger, at official events such as weddings and national occasions; the craft and customs around it were inscribed by UNESCO in 2022. The official language is Modern Standard Arabic, while daily talk uses Omani Arabic. In the south, communities also speak Modern South Arabian languages such as Mehri and Soqotri, a branch of the Afro-Asiatic family distinct from Arabic. The majlis, the room where neighbours and family gather, was recognised by UNESCO as intangible cultural heritage in 2015, with Oman among the nominating states. At the table, food is taken with the right hand.

language.note: Palestinian Arabic belongs to the Levantine Arabic group; pronunciation varies between cities, villages, and Bedouin communities.

culture_note: Guests are welcomed with ahlan wa sahlan. Near the end of a visit, the host offers a goodbye coffee; guests take their leave after drinking it. Repeatedly praising a possession is avoided, as it is believed to invite the evil eye.
people_note: Honour elders: stand when they enter and offer them a seat. Accept an offer after the host insists a second time. Use the right hand to eat and to give.

story.text: In Ramallah, guests are welcomed with the phrase ahlan wa sahlan, then shown to a seat. The host serves tea, then pastries, then coffee, following a long-established order. The bitter, cardamom-scented coffee is more than a drink; it marks the visit. Near the end of a visit, the host offers a goodbye coffee; guests take their leave after drinking it, since refusing may prolong the stay. Everyday speech here is Palestinian Arabic, part of the Levantine group, while Modern Standard Arabic is used in school and official documents. People honour their elders by standing when they enter a room and offering them a seat. Other etiquette: accept things with the right hand, and avoid praising a personal possession repeatedly, as this is believed to invite envy, the evil eye known as the ain.

language.note: Qatari Arabic belongs to the Gulf Arabic group; Modern Standard Arabic is used in media such as Al Jazeera and in administration.

culture_note: The majlis, a sitting room lined with cushions along the walls, has been listed by UNESCO as intangible heritage since 2015. There neighbours and family gather, and Arabic coffee with dates is served around the guests.
people_note: Receive and give with the right hand. Greet the eldest person first. Accept the coffee offered as a mark of respect. A calm tone and not raising one's voice are considered polite.

story.text: At Souq Waqif, the old market in Doha, Arabic coffee is poured from a long-spouted pot into small cups. Dates are served alongside. Guests accept the cup with the right hand and return it the same way. Hosts often greet a visitor with hayyak Allah, literally may God keep you, as a warm opening. Family and neighbours gather in the majlis, a sitting room lined with cushions along the walls; it has been listed by UNESCO as intangible heritage since 2015. Daily conversation in Qatar uses Gulf Arabic, while Modern Standard Arabic is used in school, official letters, and news broadcasts such as Al Jazeera. This is the situation of diglossia, two registers living side by side. The sound q commonly shifts to g and k to ch, a trait heard both on the street and in the market.

language.note: Syrian Arabic belongs to the Levantine Arabic group; its vocabulary absorbed Turkish and French words.

culture_note: Guests may arrive without an invitation; the host is expected to stop work and offer the best hospitality. Refusing an offer once, then accepting after insistence, is the polite custom.
people_note: Stand when an elder enters a room. Use the right hand to eat and to give. Do not point the soles of your feet at others. Speaking softly is considered courteous.

story.text: In Damascus, if a neighbour arrives without an invitation, the host is expected to stop work and offer the best hospitality. The custom works like this: an offer is accepted only after insistence, since a first refusal is itself a mark of good manners. Coffee is brewed strong and scented with cardamom, poured from a rakwa in the city or a long-spouted bakraj among Bedouin. The small cup is filled only partly so the host can pour again. Daily speech is Syrian Arabic, part of the Levantine group, which absorbed Turkish and French words from the region's long history. Modern Standard Arabic remains in use for official documents and teaching. At the table, the guest takes the place of honour, and elders are invited to start first. Every dish should be tasted. Speaking softly and not pointing one's feet at others are also part of social etiquette.

language.note: Yemeni Arabic is considered conservative and preserves many Classical Arabic features; Hadhrami Arabic is also spoken in Hadhramaut.

culture_note: Coffee is remembered as originating in Yemen; the word mocha refers to the port of al-Makha, and Yemeni Coffee Day is celebrated every 3 March. The upper rooms of Sana'a tower-houses are used to receive guests.
people_note: Receive and eat with the right hand. Guests are honoured and served coffee or qishr. Greet the eldest person first. Casual talk is often mixed with poetry and stories.

story.text: In Yemen, male guests are usually received in an upper room of a Sana'a tower-house, whose windows are framed with arched stained glass. There coffee is served with dates, and the small cup is filled a little at a time and refilled. Some hosts serve qishr, an infusion of coffee husks. Coffee itself is remembered as originating in Yemen: the word mocha refers to the port of al-Makha, and the country celebrates Yemeni Coffee Day every 3 March. The spice blend hawaij is added to the brew here. The official language is Modern Standard Arabic, while conversation uses Yemeni Arabic, considered conservative because it preserves many Classical Arabic features. The influence of Hadhrami Arabic, and of Malay from migration to Southeast Asia, left traces in everyday vocabulary. The right hand is used to receive and to eat.
